title: The Currency of Attention
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien argues that attention is the currency teachers trade in, and that securing it is the precondition for any learning. Drawing on Willingham's simple model of the mind, he frames attention as necessary but not sufficient, since what students attend to is only what they might learn. He organises the case around three rhyming moves, prevention, attention and retention, plus a tongue-in-cheek fourth. Prevention means stripping out decorative posters, busy slides and table groups that give students something else to attend to. Attention means winning it with silence or signals and then holding it through explicit-teaching routines that manage cognitive load. Retention means turning attended information into long-term memory through checks for understanding and spaced retrieval. The tone is humorous and anecdotal, but the argument is a coherent science-of-learning case for attention as the gateway to knowledge.
points: Attention is the gateway to learning but is worthless unless it is invested in effective teaching, because what students attend to is only what they might learn.
Prevention comes first: remove classroom clutter, over-designed slides and table groupings that compete for attention, which also reduces teacher workload.
Gaining attention needs a deliberate signal or silence with eyes up and nothing in hands; keeping it needs chunking, modelling, checks for understanding and fading scaffolds to manage cognitive load.
Passive engagement is a trap: students who look attentive may still not learn unless checks for understanding and spaced retrieval carry knowledge into long-term memory.
quotes: What we attend to, is what we (might) learn. That may be one of the hardest elements to fathom in the importance of full attention. Even with 100% attention, 100% of the time, there could be no learning occurring.
All of these elements come from a good place. They aim to celebrate and benefit the students, but they do not aid learning.

Firstly, at no time will every student have a clear viewing angle of instruction. Secondly, you may be sitting directly across from Blaze or Karizzma who will take any opportunity to distract anybody near them from the learning.

This is usually completed through all of our explicit teaching strategies such as chunking content, sequencing it carefully, relentlessly checking for understanding, modeling, gradually fading scaffolds, providing many opportunities to respond via choral response, cold calls, stop and jots etc. By doing a combination of most or all of these strategies you are likely to optimize cognitive load and therefore have the best chance of maintaining students attention and cognitive engagement in the lesson.

Attention without retention means we’re creating empty vessels. Passive engagement can be a real trap in teaching. Students who listen and look like they’re doing work, but do not seem to progress in their learning.

Painfully, that is never enough in our constant battle against forgetting as the human brain remains our nemesis in it’s ability to cull the vital information we provide it with. For retention to truly take place we must battle the forgetting curve over the coming days, weeks and months via consistent spaced retrieval to ensure that the knowledge is strongly encoded in long term memory and can be retrieved quickly and accurately.
